summary: Describes how Open Pluggable Edge Services addresses the nine architecture-level considerations raised by the Internet Architecture Board. It shows how the framework responds to the IAB's concerns.

eli5.summary: A group of advisers had nine worries about a new idea. This document answers each worry.

questions: how does opes address iab concerns
subtitle: How OPES architecture addresses concerns raised by the Internet Architecture Board.

tldr.problem: The Internet Architecture Board had nine concerns about Open Pluggable Edge Services (OPES), a framework that lets intermediaries transform content in flight. Could these boxes spy on data? Modify it without permission? Break application logic? Prevent access to unmodified content?
tldr.mechanism: This memo shows how OPES mechanisms address each concern. Key techniques include requiring one-party consent before any OPES processor touches content, making processors explicitly addressable by the client, using tracing headers so users and providers detect transformations, supporting bypass to get unmodified content, and allowing end-to-end encryption.
tldr.outcome: OPES can be deployed in ways that respect end-user and content-provider interests, though the framework acknowledges that some concerns cannot be fully eliminated (passive snooping, for example, looks like any other intermediary).

today: OPES development slowed in the mid-2000s but the framework remains relevant for Content Delivery Networks (CDNs) and inline security appliances that modify traffic. Modern approaches like service meshes and API gateways serve similar roles with different architectures. The IAB considerations raised in 2002 remain applicable to any intermediary architecture: transparency, user control, and content integrity are perennial concerns.

sections.title: The IAB Considerations and OPES Responses
sections.content:
Open Pluggable Edge Services (OPES) is a framework for deploying content adaptation at the network edge. For example, an OPES processor might compress images for slow clients, filter malware, or insert advertisements. The problem is that these intermediaries sit between content providers and consumers, potentially with power to spy, modify, or block traffic.

When OPES was proposed, the Internet Architecture Board (IAB) raised nine formal considerations. This memo responds to each one, showing how OPES mechanisms address the concern or acknowledging where the framework's guarantees are limited.

The responses fall into three categories. Some concerns are fully addressed by OPES requirements. Others are partially addressed—the framework provides tools but cannot prevent noncompliant implementations. A third category involves concerns that apply to all intermediaries, not just OPES, so OPES does not claim to solve them.
sections.eli5: OPES is a system for having boxes between you and a website modify the data flowing through. The architecture board worried about what these boxes could do. Each of the nine concerns gets an answer.

sections.title: Consent, IP Addressing, and Detectability
sections.content:
The first two considerations are about control. Consideration 2.1 (One-party consent) requires that any OPES service be explicitly authorized by either the content provider or the client. OPES architecture mandates this: processors MUST NOT process a message without consent. However, the requirement alone cannot prevent malicious actors from operating stealth processors. To address this, OPES uses content signatures (if the provider signs content, any modification breaks the signature) and encryption (if the client and provider use TLS end-to-end, they can detect tampering).

Consideration 2.2 (IP-layer communications) requires that the client be able to address OPES processors explicitly at the IP layer. OPES requires that the last processor in a chain be addressable, or that the client can reach a representative address for the entire OPES system. This prevents OPES processors from hiding—the client can send feedback or complaints to the address provided.

For internal OPES processors (running inside a content provider's own network), the framework accepts that the external address represents the whole system, even if internal processors are on private IPs. This is pragmatic: providers do not want to expose all their internal infrastructure.
sections.eli5: OPES says: You need permission before you modify anything. And the client needs to be able to point at you on the network if something goes wrong. Not all of this can be enforced, but the framework requires it.

sections.title: Notification, Tracing, and Bypass
sections.content:
Considerations 3.1 and 3.2 (Notification) address how content providers and clients detect OPES processors. The IAB wanted providers to know when their content was being modified, and clients to know when their requests were being changed.

OPES uses tracing rather than explicit notifications. When an OPES system processes an application message, it adds an OPES-System header identifying itself and what it did. This trace follows the message to the recipient. For example, an HTTP response might include OPES-System: http://www.cdn-example.com/opes/?site=7654&svc=h2t. Providers and clients can then access that URL to learn details about the transformation or file a complaint.

Traditional notifications would require a separate message flowing backward from the processor to the provider, adding complexity and overhead. Tracing piggybacks on the application message itself and scales better.

Consideration 3.3 (Non-blocking) requires that if an unmodified version of content exists, OPES MUST NOT prevent access to it. OPES supports a bypass feature: if a message includes bypass instructions, the matching OPES processor will skip processing it. Clients and providers can thus choose to avoid OPES when it is not desired.
sections.eli5: OPES adds a note to messages saying 'I changed this' and which processor did it. Providers can read that note and file a complaint. Clients and providers can also ask OPES to skip processing if they want the original unmodified version.

sections.title: URIs, References, Privacy, and Encryption
sections.content:
The next four considerations address content semantics and privacy. Consideration 4.1 (URI resolution) warns that OPES should not perform DNS lookups or URL rewrites on behalf of providers or clients. The framework does not include URI resolution as an OPES service, though implementations might do it anyway. The RFC notes that this would be outside the OPES scope and developers should discuss with the IETF if URI manipulation is needed.

Consideration 4.2 (Reference validity) requires that OPES services document how they affect links within and between documents. An OPES processor that converts HTML to plain text might break links. The framework requires that OPES tracing includes enough information for providers to understand the impact. Providers can then decide whether to block that OPES service.

Consideration 5.1 (Privacy) requires that users be able to determine the privacy policies of OPES intermediaries. OPES tracing provides identification of the processor; the client can then look up that processor's privacy statement. The framework makes identification easy but does not enforce policy compliance.

Encryption is an additional concern raised by the IAB. OPES supports hop-by-hop encryption: each link (client to processor, processor to processor, processor to provider) can use TLS. This is different from end-to-end encryption, which would encrypt content so that processors cannot see it. OPES is compatible with both: if content is encrypted end-to-end, OPES processors cannot modify it and can only act as transparent tunnels.
sections.eli5: OPES does not do DNS lookups itself. It documents how it changes content so providers know if links will break. Users can find out a processor's privacy policy by looking up the processor it identified. And if you encrypt the content all the way from sender to receiver, OPES processors cannot modify it anyway.

left.title: Traditional Notification
left.desc: Provider sends explicit message backward to OPES processor asking what happened.

right.title: OPES Tracing
right.desc: OPES processor adds identification header to the response; client reads it and looks up processor details.
